evidence.cards.0.cases.0.name.source: Eco Pulse, Malaysia: a student prototype
evidence.cards.0.cases.0.name.back: Eco Pulse, Malaysia: a prototype made by students

evidence.cards.0.cases.0.body.source: The problem: the students wanted to make recycling quicker and easier for the people who do it. Who built it: three 15-year-old students at SMK Sultan Ismail, a secondary school in Johor. What the AI does: an app looks at a photo of a recyclable item and estimates its weight and value. The evidence: it won an award in a 2024 student competition run by Samsung in Malaysia. The organiser says it is precise, but no test results have been published. A question: how well does it work with dirty or crushed items?
evidence.cards.0.cases.0.body.back: The problem: the students wanted to make recycling quicker and easier for the people who do it. Who made it: three 15-year-old students at SMK Sultan Ismail, a secondary school in Johor. What the AI does: an app looks at a photo of an item that can be recycled, then estimates its weight and value. The evidence: this app won an award in a 2024 student competition held by Samsung in Malaysia. Its organiser says this app is precise, but no test results have been published. A question: how well does this app work for items that are dirty or dented?
evidence.cards.0.cases.0.body.note: "Crushed" became "penyok" (dented), which fits bottles and cans; "SMK Sultan Ismail" is kept (in Malaysia SMK is a secondary school, unlike Indonesia's vocational SMK).

evidence.cards.0.cases.1.name.source: Traffy Fondue, Thailand: a public service in use
evidence.cards.0.cases.1.name.back: Traffy Fondue, Thailand: a public service in use

evidence.cards.0.cases.1.body.source: The problem: residents see broken roads, floods and broken street lights, and need the right office to fix them. Who built and uses it: a national science agency built it. Residents send a report with a photo and a place, and city and local offices answer. What the AI does: it sorts each report by type and sends it to the right office. People there decide what to do and do the repairs. The evidence: its makers say it received over 940,000 reports from 2022 to 2024. That shows it is used, not how well each problem was fixed. A question: how can people without a smartphone or the internet report a problem?
evidence.cards.0.cases.1.body.back: The problem: residents see broken roads, floods and broken street lights, and need the right office to repair them. Who made and uses it: a national science agency made it. Residents send a report with a photo and a location, then city and local offices respond. What the AI does: the AI sorts each report by its type and sends it to the right office. People there decide what to do and carry out the repairs. The evidence: its makers say this service received more than 940,000 reports from 2022 to 2024. That shows this service is used, not how well each problem was repaired. A question: how can people who have no smartphone or internet report a problem?

read.sections.0.heading.source: Start with the problem, not the tool
read.sections.0.heading.back: Start from the problem, not from the tool

read.sections.0.text.source: In this project, you will plan a helper for a problem that many people share in a community. Good designers start with the problem and the people it affects, not the tool. In Malaysia, three 15-year-old students wanted to make recycling easier, so they built a prototype app, Eco Pulse, that estimates the weight and value of items from a photo. Then designers ask: should AI be used here at all? AI can help when a helper must recognise or guess from many examples. But sometimes a simple rule or a person does the job better. The made-up Maple Street design club decided a tool should not choose friends, because people should choose their own.
read.sections.0.text.back: In this project, you will plan an aid tool for a problem many people have in a community. Good designers start from the problem and the people affected by it, not from the tool. In Malaysia, three 15-year-old students wanted to make recycling easier, so they made a prototype app, Eco Pulse, that estimates the weight and value of items from a photo. Then designers ask: should AI really be used here? AI can help when an aid tool must recognise or guess from many examples. But sometimes a simple rule or a human does it better. The made-up design club in Maple Street decided that a tool must not choose friends for people, because people should choose their own friends.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Designers" became "perancang"; the club is a "klub desain" (design club), the everyday word. "Friend chooser" is "alat pemilih teman".

read.sections.0.simpler.source: You will plan a helper for a shared problem. Good designers start with the problem and the people it affects. In Malaysia, three 15-year-old students wanted easier recycling. They built a prototype app, Eco Pulse. From a photo of rubbish, it tries to tell the weight and value. Should AI be used here? AI can help when a helper must learn from many examples. Sometimes a simple rule or a person is better. The made-up Maple Street club said no to a tool that chooses friends. People should choose their own.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: You will plan an aid tool for a shared problem. Good designers start from the problem and the people affected by it. In Malaysia, three 15-year-old students wanted recycling to be easier. They made a prototype app, Eco Pulse. From a photo of rubbish, the app tries to find out its weight and value. Should AI be used here? AI can help when an aid tool must learn from many examples. Sometimes a simple rule or a human is better. The made-up club in Maple Street said no to a tool that chooses friends for people. People should choose their own friends.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Plan what it learns and what could go wrong
read.sections.1.heading.back: Plan what the tool learns from and what could go wrong

read.sections.1.text.source: Next, a designer plans what the helper will learn from. The club's bin helper would learn from photos of rubbish that club members label “plastic” or “paper”. These labelled examples are its training data. As you learned in Lesson 8, a tool can fail for anything missing from its examples, so the club adds photos of crushed and dirty items too. Then the designer lists the risks: a camera near the bins must never film people's faces. Finally, the designer decides who checks the helper. The club will look inside the bins every Friday.
read.sections.1.text.back: Next, a designer plans what the aid tool will learn from. The club's bin aid tool would learn from photos of rubbish that club members label “plastic” or “paper”. These labelled examples are its training data. As you learned in Lesson 8, a tool can fail for anything that is missing from its examples, so the club also adds photos of dented and dirty items. Then the designer lists its risks: a camera near the bins must not record people's faces. Finally, the designer decides who checks the aid tool. The club will look inside the bins every Friday.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: The bin helper learns from photos of rubbish that club members label. These are its training data. A tool can fail when examples are missing. So the club adds crushed rubbish too. One risk: the camera must never film faces. Last, decide who checks it: the club looks in the bins every Friday.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: The bin aid tool learns from photos of rubbish that club members label. These photos are its training data. A tool can fail if some examples are missing. So the club also adds dented rubbish. One of its risks: the camera must not record faces. Finally, decide who checks it: the club looks inside the bins every Friday.

read.sections.2.text.source: Designers also ask what evidence shows that a helper works. Eco Pulse won a student award, but no test results have been published yet. In Thailand, Traffy Fondue's AI sorts residents' reports about problems such as floods and sends each to the right office, where people fix them. Its makers count over 940,000 reports, but a count shows use, not how well problems were fixed. Designers test their plan with users, listen to feedback, change it and test again. This is called iteration. When the club's bus-timing helper went wrong after new roadworks, they added new examples. Share your plan, change one thing, and you have version 2.
read.sections.2.text.back: Designers also ask what evidence shows that an aid tool works. Eco Pulse won a student award, but no test results have been published yet. In Thailand, Traffy Fondue's AI sorts residents' reports about problems such as floods and sends each report to the right office, where humans repair them. Its makers count more than 940,000 reports, but the number of reports shows use, not how well the problems were repaired. Designers test their plans with users, listen to feedback, change them, then test them again. This is called iteration. When the club's bus timetable aid tool went wrong after new road repairs, they added new examples. Share your plan, change one thing, and you already have version 2.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: What shows that it works? Eco Pulse won an award, but no test results are published yet. In Thailand, Traffy Fondue's AI sorts reports about problems like floods. It sends each to the right office, where people fix them. Its makers count over 940,000 reports. That shows use, not how well problems were fixed. Designers test with users, listen to feedback and change the plan. This is called iteration. Change one thing for version 2.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: What shows that the tool works? Eco Pulse won an award, but no test results have been published yet. In Thailand, Traffy Fondue's AI sorts reports about problems such as floods. That AI sends each report to the right office, where humans repair them. Its makers count more than 940,000 reports. That shows use, not how well the problems were repaired. Designers test with users, listen to feedback and change their plan. This is called iteration. Change one thing for version 2.

watch.summary.source: This short cartoon goes over the basics of AI. AI tools learn from training data. This is a large set of examples that helps them find patterns and make guesses. Some AI tools sort things or make guesses about them. Other tools, called generative AI, make new things, like writing or pictures. The video explains that AI can be very useful, but it is not perfect. It learns from what people give it, so it can repeat their mistakes. That is why the people who make and use AI need to be responsible. They need to check its answers and think about who it might affect. This is a good review before you design your own AI helper.
watch.summary.back: This short cartoon goes over the basics of AI again. AI tools learn from training data. Training data is a large collection of examples that helps the tool find patterns and make guesses. Some AI tools sort things or make guesses about them. Other tools, called generative AI, make new things, such as writing or pictures. This video explains that AI can be very useful, but it is not perfect. AI learns from what humans give it, so AI can repeat human mistakes. That is why the people who make and use AI need to be responsible. They need to check its answers and think about who might be affected. This is a good review before you design your own AI aid tool.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Problems must be ones that many people share in a community, not personal ones. Don't ask learners about problems in their own life, home or family. If a learner picks a problem about health, safety, legal matters or a particular person, gently steer them to one of the lesson's problems.

educatorNotes.0.source: This is a design on paper: nothing is built, and coding is optional. Assess five things, not how impressive or how wary the plan sounds: the need (a real problem and who it affects), the intended benefit, technical fit (why AI helps, why another way fits better, or what the learner still needs to find out: all three are strong answers), evidence and checks (how they would test it, and who checks), and one improvement after feedback. It covers UNESCO's AI system design aspect at the Understand level and touches Create. Paper version: the five steps as a worksheet. Older or more confident learners can add a test plan (which new examples, and what result would count as working) or, optionally, build a tiny sorter with Lesson 3's nearest-neighbour idea.
educatorNotes.0.back: This is a design on paper: nothing is built, and programming is optional. Assess five things, not how impressive or how careful the plan sounds: the need (a real problem and who is affected by it), the intended benefit, technical fit (why AI helps, why another way fits better, or what the learner still needs to find out: all three are strong answers), evidence and checks (how they would test it, and who checks), and one improvement after feedback. This lesson covers UNESCO's AI system design aspect at the Understand level and touches the Create level. Paper version: the five steps as a worksheet. Older or more confident learners can add a test plan (which new examples, and what result counts as working) or, if they want, build a small sorting tool with the nearest-neighbour idea from Lesson 3.
educatorNotes.0.note: UNESCO's level names are given in Indonesian with the English in brackets (Memahami/Understand, Mencipta/Create).

educatorNotes.1.source: The two real projects. Eco Pulse is known only from its organiser's account (Samsung Malaysia, 11 December 2024; also The Star, 26 January 2025): team TerraInnovators, three 15-year-olds at SMK Sultan Ismail, Johor, with an AI image-recognition app that estimates the weight and value of recyclable items, shown as a prototype at the Solve for Tomorrow 2024 final (run with Universiti Malaya). “With precision” is the organiser's claim; no test results are published, and it is not a working national service. Traffy Fondue (NECTEC, NSTDA) is an operating service: NSTDA reports over 940,000 reports from June 2022 to July 2024 and 77% “completed”, its own figures; a study of Bangkok's use (Hansen and Dahiya, 2025) notes it is digital-only, so people without smartphones or internet can be left out. Use each card's question for discussion, not as criticism of the people who built them.
educatorNotes.1.back: Those two real projects. Eco Pulse is known only from its organiser's account (Samsung Malaysia, 11 December 2024; also The Star, 26 January 2025): team TerraInnovators, three 15-year-old students at SMK Sultan Ismail, Johor, with an AI-based image recognition app that estimates the weight and value of items that can be recycled, shown as a prototype at the Solve for Tomorrow 2024 final (held with Universiti Malaya). “With precision” (precisely) is the organiser's claim; no test results have been published, and it is not a national service that is already running. Traffy Fondue (NECTEC, NSTDA) is a service that is running: NSTDA reports more than 940,000 reports from June 2022 to July 2024 and 77% with the status “completed”, by their own figures; a study of its use in Bangkok (Hansen and Dahiya, 2025) notes that the service is digital only, so people without a smartphone or internet can be left behind. Use the question on each card for discussion, not as criticism of the people who made them.
educatorNotes.1.note: The organiser's phrase "with precision" is kept in English as a quotation, with a translation.
